content.text: Melting points: SiO₂ melts at about 1700 °C and Cu at about 1085 °C, so SiO₂ is higher.

answers.final_answer: Solid SiO₂ is made of Si and O atoms joined in a continuous 3‑D network. Each Si is bonded to 4 O atoms and each O to 2 Si atoms. Strong covalent bonds, made of shared electron pairs, hold the atoms in place.

answers.brief_reasoning: Mobile delocalized electrons in metal; localized electrons in network
answers.final_answer: Solid Cu conducts electricity well, and solid SiO₂ does not, because it is an insulator. Cu is a lattice of Cu cations surrounded by a sea of delocalized valence electrons. These electrons can move freely through the solid and carry charge. In SiO₂ the electrons are held in localized covalent bonds between atoms. There are no ions or electrons free to move, so no current flows.

SiO₂ has the higher melting point. To melt SiO₂, many strong, directional Si–O covalent bonds throughout the network must be broken. In Cu, the metal cations can slide past one another while the metallic bonding is only partly weakened, so less energy is needed. (Measured values: SiO₂ ≈ 1700 °C, Cu ≈ 1085 °C.)

answers.brief_reasoning: Both are nonpolar, so London dispersion forces are the only intermolecular forces. Butane has more electrons and a bigger electron cloud, which makes it more polarizable and gives it stronger LDFs.
answers.final_answer: Butane boils at 273 K, which is higher than propane at 231 K. Both molecules are nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces hold them together. Butane is larger, with more electrons and a more polarizable electron cloud (and more surface contact), so its dispersion forces are stronger. More energy is needed to overcome them, so its boiling point is higher.

answers.brief_reasoning: The hydrogen bond forms between the H on one ethanol's O and a lone pair on the O of the other ethanol.
answers.final_answer: CH3CH2–O–H ····· :O(H)–CH2CH3. The dashed line runs from the hydroxyl H of molecule 1 to a lone pair on the O of molecule 2, and the O–H···O atoms are close to a straight line.

answers.brief_reasoning: Ethanol has an O–H bond, so it can hydrogen bond. Dimethyl ether has no H on its O, so it has only dipole-dipole forces and LDFs.
answers.final_answer: Ethanol has an H bonded directly to a very electronegative O atom, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other. Dimethyl ether's H atoms are all bonded to C, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself. It has only weaker dipole–dipole forces and London dispersion forces, which are similar to ethanol's because the two compounds have the same molar mass. Ethanol's hydrogen bonds are stronger, so more energy is needed to separate its molecules, and it boils at 351 K compared with 248 K for dimethyl ether.

answers.brief_reasoning: MgO is made of Mg2+ cations and O2- anions arranged in a 3-D lattice. Strong electrostatic (Coulombic) attractions between the oppositely charged ions hold them in place. This is ionic bonding.
answers.final_answer: Mg2+ and O2- ions held in a lattice by strong Coulombic attractions between oppositely charged ions (ionic bonds)

answers.brief_reasoning: Ag has a sea of delocalized valence electrons that can move freely through the lattice of Ag+ cations, so it conducts electricity. In solid MgO the ions are locked in fixed lattice positions, and the electrons are localized on the ions, so no charged species can move.
answers.final_answer: Solid Ag conducts electricity well; solid MgO does not. Ag has mobile delocalized electrons, while the ions in solid MgO are fixed in place and it has no free electrons.

answers.brief_reasoning: Mg2+ and O2- have high charges (2+ and 2-) and small radii, so the Coulombic attraction between them is very strong. Melting MgO takes much more energy than overcoming the metallic bonding between Ag+ cations and the electron sea. Actual melting points: MgO about 2850 °C, Ag about 962 °C.
answers.final_answer: MgO has the higher melting point, because of the very strong attractions between its small, highly charged 2+ and 2- ions

answers.brief_reasoning: Covalent network solid: neutral Si and C atoms in an extended 3-D lattice, each atom covalently bonded to neighbors (tetrahedral).
answers.final_answer: Solid SiC is made of Si and C atoms. Each atom is held in place by covalent bonds (shared electron pairs) to four neighboring atoms, forming a continuous 3-D network.

answers.brief_reasoning: Metals have a sea of delocalized electrons that can move; in SiC the electrons are localized in covalent bonds and there are no mobile ions or electrons.
answers.final_answer: Solid Fe conducts electricity well, but solid SiC is a poor conductor (it is a semiconductor or insulator). In Fe, the valence electrons are delocalized in a 'sea' around the Fe cations and can move when a voltage is applied. In SiC, the valence electrons are held in localized covalent bonds between specific atoms, and there are no free ions, so no charged particles can move freely.

answers.brief_reasoning: Melting SiC means breaking many strong covalent bonds throughout the network. SiC melts or decomposes at about 2700 °C; Fe melts at about 1538 °C.
answers.final_answer: SiC has the higher melting point. To melt SiC, many strong, directional covalent bonds across the whole network must be broken. To melt Fe, the metal cations only have to overcome metallic attractions to the electron sea well enough to slide past each other, which takes less energy.
